name: Chitwan & the Terai
tagline: Rhinos, Tharu villages and Sita's Mithila
meta_description: Chitwan and the Terai: rhino safaris, Tharu villages, gharials at Kasara, Janakpur's Janaki Mandir, Mithila painting and Koshi Tappu's wild buffalo.
summary: Chitwan and the Terai are Nepal's flat, warm south: sal forest and tall grass where one-horned rhinos and tigers live, Tharu villages along the Rapti and Narayani, and the Mithila plains of Janakpur, Sita's city. Go October to March, give Chitwan two or three nights and add Janakpur or Koshi Tappu for culture and birds.
intro: Most people picture Nepal as mountains, then land at Bharatpur and find a valley floor at about 150 metres, flat as a plate, with elephant grass taller than a jeep. This is the Terai and the Inner Terai: the strip of plains and river valleys that runs the length of the country along the Indian border. Chitwan sits in a pocket between the Mahabharat range and the Siwalik hills, and it holds Nepal's first national park, set up in 1973 and listed by UNESCO in 1984.

We send most travellers to Chitwan for wildlife, and they are rarely disappointed. Chitwan National Park and its buffer zone hold most of Nepal's greater one-horned rhinos, a healthy tiger population, gaur, sloth bear, four kinds of deer, two kinds of crocodile and more than 540 recorded bird species. You see them from a jeep, a dugout canoe on the Rapti, a machan tower or on foot with two licensed nature guides.

The other half of this region is the Mithila plains to the east. Janakpur, capital of Madhesh Province, is the city Hindus know as the home of Sita, with the white Janaki Mandir at its heart and more than 200 sacred ponds around it. Women here paint the walls of their homes in the Mithila style. Further east, the Koshi river spreads over a wide floodplain at Koshi Tappu, where Nepal's last wild water buffalo graze among reeds.

Plan on heat and dust from April, monsoon rain from mid-June to September, and cool, foggy mornings in December and January. The roads are flat but busy; flights to Bharatpur, Simara, Janakpur and Biratnagar take 20 to 40 minutes from Kathmandu. A first visit fits in three nights at Chitwan; a fuller trip adds a Tharu homestay, Devghat, Janakpur and Koshi Tappu over eight to ten nights. Most of our guests combine Chitwan with Kathmandu and Pokhara.

story.title: From malaria forest to rhino country
paras: For centuries the Terai was a belt of sal forest and swamp that hill people called the Char Kose Jhadi, the forest four kos deep. Malaria made it deadly for outsiders, and it served as a natural wall between the hill kingdoms and the plains of India. The people who lived inside it were the Tharu, who farmed clearings, fished the rivers and built houses of mud-plastered reed. Medical studies later showed why they survived: malaria strikes Tharu about seven times less often than their neighbours, linked to thalassemia genes found in nearly all Tharu tested.

From the late 19th century Chitwan became the winter hunting ground of Nepal's rulers. Rana prime ministers set up grand camps for weeks at a time and hosted foreign royalty, including King George V in December 1911, when dozens of tigers and rhinos were shot. The forest stayed thick because few others could live in it. In 1950 Chitwan's forests and grasslands still covered more than 2,600 square kilometres and held about 800 rhinos. Tharu families lived on the forest's edges, working for the hunting camps and farming their clearings.

Then everything changed quickly. DDT spraying in the 1950s and 1960s cleared malaria, a resettlement programme brought thousands of families down from the hills, and by the end of the 1960s about 70 per cent of the jungle was gone and only 95 rhinos were left. The government sent out the Gaida Gasti, an armed rhino patrol, and gazetted Chitwan National Park, established in 1973. Tharu villages inside the new boundary were cleared, a loss many families still speak about. The rhinos came back: Nepal has since marked full years with no rhino poached at all.

East of Chitwan the story is older and written in stone and verse. From 1097 to 1324 the Karnata kings ruled Mithila from the fortified city of Simraungadh in today's Bara district, and the first known work of Maithili prose, the Varna Ratnakara, was written under them. Janakpur grew in the 18th century around the place pilgrims honour as Sita's birthplace, and in 1910 to 1911 Queen Vrisha Bhanu of Tikamgarh completed the Janaki Mandir there. Today Maithili, Bhojpuri, Tharu and Nepali are all spoken within a day's drive of each other.

legend: In the Ramayana, King Janaka of Videha was ploughing a field as part of a ritual when his plough struck a golden casket in the furrow. Inside lay a baby girl. He named her Sita, from the word for furrow, and raised her as his daughter. Years later he set a test for her suitors: whoever could string the great bow of Shiva would marry her. Only Rama could lift it, and it snapped in his hands. Janakpur claims the palace, Dhanusha Dham claims a piece of the broken bow.
people: The Tharu are the oldest people of the Chitwan valley and the wider Terai, speaking Tharu languages and farming rice, mustard and lentils. Bote, Musahar, Darai and Kumal families have long fished and ferried on the Narayani and Rapti. Since the 1950s Brahmin, Chhetri, Gurung, Magar and Tamang settlers from the hills have farmed Chitwan. In the east, Maithili-speaking Maithil communities fill Janakpur and Dhanusha, Bhojpuri is the home language around Simraungadh, and Kochila Tharu live near Koshi Tappu.

untold.fact: Researchers comparing the Tharu with neighbouring groups in the Terai found malaria nearly seven times less common among Tharu, and follow-up work found thalassemia genes in almost all Tharu studied, a likely reason they could live in the malarial forest.
Chitwan held about 800 rhinos in 1950, but after malaria eradication and resettlement only 95 remained by the end of the 1960s, which pushed the government to create Nepal's first national park.
Chitwan National Park, Parsa National Park and India's Valmiki National Park join to form one block of protected forest of about 2,075 square kilometres, so tigers and rhinos cross the border freely.
Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve was designated a Ramsar wetland of international importance in December 1987, Nepal's first Ramsar site, and it holds the country's only wild water buffalo.

untold.fact: Nepal's only working passenger railway runs on the plains of Mithila, from Jaynagar in Bihar across the border to Janakpur and beyond, on a line first opened in the 1930s.

taste.name: Ghonghi
taste.text: Tharu households collect ghonghi, freshwater snails, from flooded rice fields and cook them with garlic, chilli and spices, then suck the meat from the shell. Ask for a Tharu thali at a homestay in Barauli or Amaltari, or at Tharu-run kitchens in Sauraha, and it often comes with dhikri and greens.

highlights.title: Rhinos at dawn in Chitwan
highlights.text: Chitwan holds most of Nepal's greater one-horned rhinos. Early jeep drives and canoe trips on the Rapti give the best odds, and in February and March the cut grasslands make them easy to see. Tigers are present but shy; count any sighting as a bonus.

highlights.title: A night in a Tharu village
highlights.text: Community homestays at Barauli and Amaltari on the western edge of the park are run by Tharu families. You eat at their table, walk the mustard fields, watch the stick dance and learn how a mud-and-reed house stays cool in May.

highlights.title: Gharials at Kasara
highlights.text: The breeding centre at the park headquarters in Kasara hatches eggs of the critically endangered gharial, a slim-snouted, fish-eating crocodile, and raises the young for several years before releasing them into the Narayani and Rapti.

highlights.title: Birds of Bishazari Tal
highlights.text: Bishazari Tal, the 'twenty thousand lakes', is a Ramsar-listed oxbow wetland in the park's buffer zone. Winter brings ducks, storks and eagles, and mugger crocodiles bask on the banks a short walk from Bharatpur.

highlights.title: Janakpur, Sita's city
highlights.text: The white marble Janaki Mandir, finished in 1910 to 1911, the wedding pavilion, and sacred ponds such as Ganga Sagar make Janakpur the heart of Mithila. Visit a women's painting centre to see Mithila art made by hand.

highlights.title: Koshi Tappu's wild buffalo
highlights.text: On the Koshi floodplain, reed beds and channels shelter Nepal's last arna, wild water buffalo, plus gharial, river dolphins and one of the country's richest bird lists. Winter boat trips and walks along the embankment are the way to see them.

getting_there: Chitwan is about 150 to 170 km from Kathmandu: 5 to 7 hours by road via Mugling and Narayangadh, or a 20 to 25 minute flight to Bharatpur (BHR), then 30 minutes by car to Sauraha. Pokhara to Sauraha is about 150 km, 5 to 6 hours. Tourist buses run daily from both cities. For Janakpur, fly about 25 to 30 minutes from Kathmandu, or drive about 225 km on the BP Highway through Sindhuli, 6 to 8 hours. Parsa and Simraungadh are reached via Simara airport (SIF) or Hetauda. For Koshi Tappu, fly to Biratnagar (BIR) and drive about 1.5 to 2 hours. Road travel slows during monsoon landslides on the Mugling stretch; check current status before you travel.
permits: There is no special permit for the Terai, but every national park and reserve charges a daily entry fee, collected at the gate or bought through your lodge. For Chitwan we understand the foreign visitor rate to be about NPR 2,000 per person per day, with lower rates for SAARC and Nepali visitors. Walks inside parks must be led by licensed nature guides, usually two per group. Nepal's April 2023 rule requiring foreign trekkers in national parks and conservation areas to use a licensed guide also applies. Check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Chitwan 7–23 °C, dry, thick fog until mid-morning
months.summary: Cool, dry and quiet in the park. Fog can sit on the Rapti until ten, so morning canoe trips feel ghostly and afternoon drives see more. Maghi falls in mid-January, when Tharu families hold their new year feasts and pilgrims bathe at Devghat. Around this time locals are allowed into the park for a short season of grass cutting, which starts to open the views. Janakpur is cold at night; pack a fleece.
months.tip: Book afternoon jeep drives rather than dawn ones in January, when fog hides the grasslands.

months.summary: Our favourite month for wildlife. The grass has been cut, the mornings clear sooner, and rhinos graze in the open along the Rapti. Migrant birds are still at Bishazari Tal and Koshi Tappu, and the days are warm enough to sit in a canoe without shivering. Tharu villages are planting and harvesting mustard, so the fields around Barauli and Amaltari are yellow. Koshi Tappu's migrant birds are at their peak.
months.tip: Combine Chitwan with Koshi Tappu now, while both the wildlife and the migrant birds are at their best.

months.summary: Hot afternoons, cool dawns and excellent sightings. Animals gather near water as the forest dries, and the sal trees drop their leaves, which opens views in the forest. Holi arrives in March in most years and is celebrated loudly in Janakpur and across the Terai; expect coloured powder on the roads. Book Chitwan lodges early, as this is a busy month. Koshi Tappu and Bishazari Tal still hold many winter birds, and the first heat of spring brings animals to water.
months.tip: Plan wildlife activities for dawn and late afternoon and rest at midday, when the heat climbs past 30 °C.

months.summary: Hot and dry, with pre-monsoon thunderstorms in the late afternoons. Wildlife sightings stay good around water, and tiger chances are as good as they get because animals keep to the few remaining pools. Fewer travellers mean quieter lodges and easier bookings. Janakpur and Koshi Tappu are very hot by midday; go early and keep to the shade. Koshi Tappu is still good for birds early in the month, though most winter migrants have left by April.
months.tip: Choose a lodge with a fan or air conditioning and keep outdoor plans to before 10 am and after 4 pm.

months.summary: The hottest month. Temperatures pass 35 °C most days and humidity rises ahead of the monsoon. The park is open and rhinos wallow in plain sight, but sitting in a jeep at noon is hard work. We only suggest May for travellers who handle heat well and want lower rates. Devghat and Janakpur are best kept to early mornings. Bring light, long-sleeved clothing for sun and insects, and plan a rest at midday in your lodge.
months.tip: Carry at least 3 litres of water per person each day and an electrolyte sachet or two.

months.summary: The monsoon usually breaks around the middle of June. Rivers rise, grass grows fast and many jungle lodges close until autumn. Leeches appear on forest trails. Rice planting fills the Tharu fields with people, which is a fine thing to see from a car window, but this is not a wildlife month. Lodges cut their rates and some close in late May or June, so confirm before you book.
months.tip: If you travel in June, confirm your lodge is open and which park activities are still running.

months.summary: The wettest stretch of the year. Most of the annual 2,500 mm of rain falls between mid-June and September, and the Narayani, Rapti and Koshi run high and brown. Park access is limited and floods can close roads. We do not recommend Chitwan or Koshi Tappu now; Janakpur's temples stay open for pilgrims. Janakpur and Devghat stay open for pilgrims, and the green paddy fields are at their most vivid, but road travel is slow.
months.tip: Allow a spare day for road delays in July and keep valuables in dry bags.

months.summary: Still the monsoon. The landscape is intensely green, the rivers are wide and the grass is too tall to see over. Some lodges in Sauraha stay open with village walks, cycling and cultural programmes, but wildlife viewing is poor and many park roads are closed. The Mugling road can be cut by landslides. If you must travel, keep to towns and temples and allow spare days for delays.
months.tip: If the road is blocked, the 20 minute flight to Bharatpur is the reliable option.

months.weather: Chitwan 24–33 °C, rain easing late in the month
months.summary: The monsoon eases in the second half of the month and lodges reopen. Grass is at its tallest, so sightings are harder, but birds are active and the air is clear after rain. Dashain often falls in late September or October and roads fill with families going home. Book transport early. Leeches, humidity and closed roads make walking in the forest unpleasant until the rains end.
months.tip: Check Dashain dates for the year and book buses or flights at least two weeks ahead.

months.summary: Dry season returns. Skies clear, rivers drop and the park opens fully. Grass is still tall early in the month, so canoe trips and jungle walks are more rewarding than jeep drives. Dashain and Tihar fill October and early November, and Chhath follows six days after Tihar's Laxmi Puja, sometimes in late October. By the end of the month most park activities resume, though jungle walks are wet and the grass tall.
months.tip: Combine Chitwan with Pokhara now; both are at their clearest after the monsoon.

months.summary: Excellent all round. Days are warm, nights cool and the first winter birds arrive at Bishazari Tal and Koshi Tappu. Chhath lights up the ghats of Janakpur in early to mid-November in most years, and Vivaha Panchami, the re-enacted wedding of Rama and Sita, falls in late November or December. Mid-month onward, park roads reopen and the first winter birds return to the wetlands.
months.tip: For Chhath in Janakpur, book rooms well ahead and be at Ganga Sagar before dawn on the final morning.

months.summary: Cool and calm, with fog starting to settle on the valley floor late in the month. Wildlife viewing is good, and winter ducks crowd the wetlands. Vivaha Panchami often falls in early December, when Janakpur hosts the wedding procession of Rama and Sita. Bring warm layers for morning canoe trips. December nights are cool, so pack layers for dawn activities.
months.tip: Pack a warm jacket and hat for dawn activities; the river air is colder than the thermometer suggests.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Chitwan?
faqs.a: Two nights is the minimum and three is better. With three nights you get a canoe trip on the Rapti, a full or half-day jeep drive, a guided jungle walk and a Tharu village visit without rushing. Add a fourth night if you want to split your stay between Sauraha and a quieter lodge in Meghauli or Amaltari, or add a night at Bishazari Tal for birding.

faqs.q: What is the best time to see rhinos and tigers in Chitwan?
faqs.a: February to April is best. The grass is cut in January and February, the forest thins as it dries, and animals gather near water. Rhinos are seen on most trips from October to April. Tigers are present in good numbers but are shy, and sightings are never guaranteed even on a full-day drive. Avoid June to August, when rain and tall grass hide everything.

faqs.q: Is Chitwan better than Bardia for wildlife?
faqs.a: Chitwan is easier to reach and almost certain for rhinos, birds and crocodiles, with lodges for every budget. Bardia, in the far west, is quieter, wilder and often better for tiger sightings, but it takes a long drive or a flight to Nepalgunj. For a first trip to Nepal with limited days we suggest Chitwan; repeat visitors who want solitude often prefer Bardia.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide in Chitwan National Park?
faqs.a: Yes. All activities inside the park, including jungle walks, canoe trips and jeep drives, must be done with licensed nature guides, and walks usually need two guides per group. Nepal's April 2023 rule also requires foreign trekkers in national parks to use a licensed guide. Your lodge arranges guides and permits as part of the package. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk in the jungle in Chitwan?
faqs.a: Guided walks are generally safe when you follow your guides closely, keep quiet and stay together. Rhinos, sloth bears and wild elephants can charge, and guides brief you on what to do: climb a tree, move behind a large trunk or zigzag. Do not walk alone in the park or the buffer zone forests, and avoid walking at dusk.

faqs.q: How do I get from Kathmandu to Chitwan?
faqs.a: Fly 20 to 25 minutes to Bharatpur and drive about 30 minutes to Sauraha, or go by road, about 165 km and 5 to 7 hours via Mugling and Narayangadh. Tourist buses leave Kathmandu each morning and drop passengers near Sauraha. A private car is more comfortable and lets you stop at Devghat or the Kurintar cable car station on the way.

faqs.q: Is Janakpur worth visiting from Chitwan?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are interested in Hindu pilgrimage, Mithila painting or Terai town life. Janakpur is very different from Chitwan: crowded, devotional and full of colour. It is about 7 to 8 hours east by road, so most people fly from Kathmandu instead. One full day covers the Janaki Mandir, the ponds and a painting centre; two lets you add Dhanusha Dham.

faqs.q: What should I pack for Chitwan and the Terai?
faqs.a: Neutral-coloured clothes in green, brown or khaki for safaris, long sleeves and trousers against mosquitoes, a hat, sunglasses and sunscreen. Bring insect repellent, a torch, binoculars and comfortable closed shoes for jungle walks. From December to February add a warm jacket and hat for foggy mornings. In temples in Janakpur, cover shoulders and knees and remove shoes.

Malaria was eradicated from most of the Terai in the 1950s and 1960s, and the risk to travellers today is low, but dengue and occasional malaria cases are reported in and after the monsoon. Use repellent at dawn and dusk, sleep under a net or in screened rooms, and talk to a travel clinic about your own needs before you travel.
